analysis.one_liner: Temporarily caps credit card interest rates at 10%.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2025 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has received no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the federal Truth in Lending Act to make it illegal for credit card companies to charge an annual interest rate above 10%, including all finance charges, and would stop them from stacking fees on top to get around the cap. If a lender knowingly overcharges, it forfeits all the interest on the debt, and cardholders can sue to recover what they paid for two years after the overcharge. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission would enforce the cap under existing Truth in Lending rules, and the whole cap would end on January 1, 2031. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 100 million American households that carry a credit card balance month to month, most of whom currently pay far above 10% — average card rates have run near or above 20%. It also lets borrowers sue to claw back interest and fees charged above the cap, with penalties enforced by the CFPB and FTC. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 10%, inclusive of all finance charges.
Prevents lenders from using fees to evade the cap, limiting non-finance-charge fees so their total cannot exceed the finance charges assessed.
A creditor that knowingly overcharges forfeits the entire interest on the debt, and a cardholder can sue within two years to recover all interest, finance charges, or fees paid.

Violations are subject to civil liability under the Truth in Lending Act, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission, and the bill does not preempt state laws that protect consumers more.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — large banks and finance companies that earn interest and fee income from card balances, currently priced well above 10% for many borrowers. Under the cap their lending revenue from cards would fall sharply, which is why the banking industry would be expected to fight it. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The cap is temporary: every provision sunsets on January 1, 2031, so relief would last only a few years unless Congress renewed it.

A hard cap can cut off credit rather than lower its price: issuers who cannot charge riskier borrowers a rate matching their risk may reduce credit lines, tighten approval, or pull out of serving customers with weak credit, leaving some borrowers with fewer options rather than cheaper ones. (This is a general effect of binding interest rate caps, not a claim in the bill text.)

The cap does not distinguish between borrowers: a cardholder who pays in full each month, and one carrying high-risk debt, face the same 10% ceiling, so lenders may respond by reducing rewards or imposing other charges for everyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying balances at 20% or more interest, a 10% cap would be a large, direct saving, backed by real enforcement teeth — forfeiting all interest on overcharges and a private right to sue. The honest cost is on the supply side: lenders unable to price risk may ration credit, and people with poor credit could find cards harder to get even as the cards get cheaper. The five-year sunset limits both the benefit and the disruption. Whether the trade is worth it depends heavily on how issuers respond, which the bill does not address.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in February 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill with Senator Josh Hawley on February 4, 2025.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
That referral is the last recorded action; the committee has held no hearing, marked up no version, and no vote has occurred.
The Congress runs until January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive, but with no committee action it has no visible path to a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, who so far face no cap on rates that for many cardholders run above 20%, because the bill has gone nowhere in committee.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and has pressed for capping card rates at 10%.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer, giving it a Republican as well as an independent sponsor.

for.name: Additional cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill after introduction.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking industry groups
against.role: Lenders who would lose interest and fee revenue under a 10% cap
against.what_they_did: Would be expected to oppose the bill; industry opposition to rate caps is standard, though the congressional record here does not document it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan — an independent sponsor joined by a Republican co-introducer and three cosponsors split 2 Democrats and 1 Republican — but no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of the chamber is unknown.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Banking Committee with no hearing or markup scheduled. Most Senate bills referred to committee and untouched in their first year never reach the floor; unless the committee schedules action or the sponsors force the issue, this one is likely to remain pending and expire at the end of the 119th Congress.
